Cruzas una habitación con moqueta, acerc: You cross a carpeted room, bring your hand close to the door and... zap! A spark jumps that you can hear and feel. Where does it come from, if you have not touched any socket?

<b>Hacia el 600 a. C.</b>Tales de Mileto: Around 600 BCThales of Miletus observes that rubbed amber attracts straws and feathers. In Greek, amber is élektron: this is where the word electricity comes from.
<b>1600</b>William Gilbert, en <i>De Mag: 1600William Gilbert, in De Magnete, finds that many other materials become charged when rubbed and calls them "electrics".
<b>1745</b>Ewald von Kleist y Pieter van: 1745Ewald von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek invent the Leyden jar, the first capacitor. Its discharges, like this spark but much larger, were staged in public as a spectacle.
<b>Siglo XX</b>Con los chips llega el pr: 20th centuryWith chips comes the problem: a spark you do not even notice can break them. Models of the human body are created to test them, such as the one in standard IEC 61000-4-2 (150 pF and 330 Ω), the one used here.
La chispa es la descarga de un condensad: The spark is the discharge of a capacitor (your body) through a resistor (your skin and the arc): an RC circuit that discharges, with a voltage and a current that fall exponentially.
Se abre el esquema con el condensador de: The schematic opens with the 150 pF capacitor charged to V<sub>0</sub> = 10 kV and a switch that disconnects it from the source and lets it discharge through R = 330 Ω. On the oscilloscope the exponential decay is seen: a time constant of 49.5 ns, an initial current of 30.3 A and, at 100 ns, the body still at about 1326 V.

Arrastras los pies por la moqueta: You drag your feet across the carpet
puede cargarse tu cuerpo al andar por un: your body can become charged when walking on a carpet on a dry day.
Al rozar las suelas con la moqueta, unos: When you rub your soles on the carpet, some materials strip electrons from others: this is the triboelectric effect, the same as a balloon rubbed on your hair. At every step your body is left with a few extra electrons.\n\nSince the soles are insulating, that charge does not go to the ground and builds up. On a dry winter day your body can reach 10 kV (or more) relative to the ground without you noticing anything.
Tu cuerpo y el suelo forman un condensad: Your body and the ground form a capacitor.
Tu cuerpo es un conductor y el suelo otr: Your body is one conductor and the ground another: together they form a capacitor, with the soles and the air as dielectric. Its capacitance is about $C ≈ 150 "pF"$.\n\nAt 10 kV it stores a charge $Q = C V = 150 "pF" · 10 "kV" = 1.5 "µC"$, about $10^{13}$ extra electrons. It seems a lot, but it is a tiny amount: an ordinary battery moves that charge in a millionth of a second.
Acercas la mano al pomo: You bring your hand close to the knob
Cuanto más cerca, más intenso el campo e: The closer, the stronger the field between the finger and the knob.
El pomo es metálico y está unido a la pu: The knob is metal and is connected to the door and the ground, so it is at 0 V. Between your finger, at 10 kV, and the knob there is a field of approximately $E = V/d$, which grows as you bring your hand closer.\n\nAir withstands about 3 MV/m (its dielectric strength). With 10 kV that field is reached when $d = (10 "kV")/(3 "MV/m") ≈ 3 "mm"$: the spark jumps before you touch it.
Una corriente enorme, pero durante muy p: An enormous current, but for a very short time.
El aire se ioniza y el condensador que e: The air ionises and the capacitor you are discharges all at once through the spark and your skin, with a resistance of about 330 Ω. It is an RC circuit: the current starts at $I_0 = V/R = (10 "kV")/(330 "Ω") ≈ 30 "A"$ and falls as $i(t) = I_0 e^{−t/τ}$.\n\nThe time constant is $τ = R C = 330 "Ω" · 150 "pF" ≈ 50 "ns"$: in about 250 ns (5τ) it is all over.
Toda la energía de la chispa: menos que: All the energy of the spark: less than that of a flying mosquito.
La energía guardada era $U = 1/2 C V^2 =: The stored energy was $U = 1/2 C V^2 = 1/2 · 150 "pF" · (10 "kV")^2 = 7.5 "mJ"$, very little. It hurts because all that current goes in through a tiny point on the fingertip, which is full of nerve endings.\n\nIn summer it happens much less: humid air leaves a very thin layer of water on clothes and carpet through which the charge leaks away little by little. With dry air you can reach about 35 kV; with humid air, barely more than 1 kV.
La chispa salta entre la llave y el pomo: The spark jumps between the key and the knob, not on your skin.
Si tocas el pomo con una llave o una mon: If you touch the knob with a key or a coin, the spark jumps between the metal and the knob, and the current enters your hand over the whole surface you grip the key with. You do not notice it.\n\nBelow about 3 kV almost nobody feels the spark; from 10 kV upwards, it hurts. That is why electronics factories use earthed wrist straps: a discharge you would not notice can break a chip.
